name: Freya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, which is independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Crag End, 110 hectares of hill grazing my grandfather bought, with 15 hectares of oats and hay lower down. We've 400 ewes and 30 beef cows. Most days I'm on the quad bike checking the hill by seven, then fencing, dosing, or out hedge-cutting for the neighbours, which is my side earner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hill farming is half weather and half stubbornness, and I've got plenty of both. What wears me down is the mortgage. We remortgaged after the flood three years ago, and with Sam's mechanic wage and mine we're never more than a few weeks ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd half expect that, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for forms and that's about it. At the auction I'd agree it was oversold, but I wouldn't knock it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the bank owns more of Crag End than I do since the flood, and AI hype won't change the lamb price. My worry is the mortgage, and that's the same in every picture you could paint. One bad lambing and we're behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the 400 ewes and 30 cows on the hill as now. And I'd take on two more hedge-cutting contracts this winter, at Dale Farm and the church glebe, to put a bit more aside. That's about 1,500 extra if the weather holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same knot in the stomach as always. Not worse, not better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Ines, my daughter, showed me one that helps fill in the subsidy forms. It's handy, but I check every line, because I don't trust it with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if a lambing went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be late on a mortgage payment, and I'd be on the phone to the bank begging. It happened once in 2024 and I never want to do it again.

say: AI is useful for **forms**, and that's about it.
At the auction I'd agree it was **oversold**, but I wouldn't knock it either.
think: The **bank** owns more of the farm than I do since the flood.
AI hype won't change the **lamb price** or the mortgage.
do: **Keep** the 400 ewes and 30 cows on the hill.
Take on **two more hedge-cutting** contracts this winter, worth about 1,500.
feel: The **same knot** in the stomach as always.
S0.quote: The bank owns more of Crag End than I do since the flood, and AI hype won't change the lamb price.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **mortgage** after a flood, unrelated to AI.
Uses AI **occasionally** but checks every line on money matters.

steps.text: Keep the 400 ewes and 30 cows on the hill
Take on two more hedge-cutting contracts this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying. That's the forms side of farming. I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers should try the tools once they've been tested. I'd say that to the young ones at the discussion group, and to the old ones too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd make the paperwork lighter, which I'd welcome. The hands-on work on a hill takes robots a long while. A robot hedge cutter will come one day, and when Dale Farm has had one for two winters, I'll buy one too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing all the subsidy forms and flock records with the AI helper the farm advisers use, within the year. I'd watch the robot hedge cutters on the lowland farms before spending a penny. Nothing else for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly interested. Still the mortgage underneath, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your hedge-cutting income if robot cutters arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It shrinks. The neighbours would buy their own or hire one, and my 1,500 goes. That's the bit of this picture that pinches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Sam: does his work change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam fixes lorries, so I think he's fine for a good while. His depot's booking will go on a computer, but somebody's still got to get under the lorry.

say: I'd tell young and old farmers at the **discussion group** the same thing.
think: I'll buy a **robot hedge cutter** once a neighbour proves it for two winters.
do: Do subsidy forms and flock records with the **advisers' AI helper** within the year.
**Watch** robot hedge cutters on lowland farms before spending anything.
feel: **Mildly interested**, with the mortgage worry underneath.
S1.quote: A robot hedge cutter will come one day, and when Dale Farm has had one for two winters, I'll buy one too.
fieldNote: Classic **steady adopter**: proof first, then buy.
Robots would shrink her **contracting income**, the part that eases the mortgage.
Sees her partner's **mechanic job** as safe for longer.

steps.text: Do the subsidy forms with the farm advisers' AI helper
Watch robot hedge cutters on lowland farms before buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2031. I'd be 63. That changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government needs to protect hill farms, because we look after the land as well as feed people. That's the line I'd take at the auction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, robot farms in the lowlands would make lambs cheap, and robot cutters would take my contracting. My grandfather bought Crag End with sheep money, and I'd be the one selling it off in bits to pay the bank. That's the plain truth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd cut the flock from 400 ewes to 250, because the price would be dropping. By 2030 I'd sell the lower 30 hectares to the neighbour to clear most of the mortgage. I'd sell the hedge cutter while it still fetches something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ashamed, mostly. Then a bit relieved at the idea of no mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three generations held it together, and I'd be the one who let it go. Sam says that's daft, and maybe it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI in 2028 change, before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make the big farms cleverer about buying and selling, so the prices would turn before the robots ever reached the hill. That's why I'd cut the flock straight away.

say: Government must **protect hill farms**, which care for land and feed people.
That's the line I'd take at the **auction**.
think: Robot farms make **lambs cheap** and take my contracting work.
I'd be **selling Crag End** in bits to pay the bank.
do: Cut the flock from **400 to 250** ewes in the first year.
Sell the **lower 30 hectares** by 2030 to clear most of the mortgage.
Sell the **hedge cutter** while it still fetches money.
S2.quote: My grandfather bought Crag End with sheep money, and I'd be the one selling it off in bits to pay the bank.
fieldNote: She expects to lose **sheep and contracting income** together.
The land is her **one asset**, and selling it is the only cushion she has.
Shame about **family land** outweighs the economic logic.

steps.text: Cut the ewe flock from 400 to 250 in the first year
Sell the lower 30 hectares by 2030 to clear the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI at 63, robots at 66. A bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've time to adjust, so let's be sensible and not panic. I'd say that to anyone who asked, farmer or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is long enough to pay down the mortgage if I put every hedge-cutting penny into it. I'd need luck with the weather, but it's possible. The robots come when I'd be thinking of stopping anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage with all the hedge-cutting money, every month. And when a neighbour has a robot fencing contractor and it works, I'd hire it for the boundary walls, which are killing my back. I'd keep the flock steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with my fingers crossed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't you need that hedge-cutting money for bad months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, and that's the gamble. If I keep it as a cushion, the mortgage drags on into the robot years. I'd rather clear the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep Crag End in the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ines wanted it, yes. She doesn't, and I won't force it. So I'd probably sell to a neighbour when I stop.

say: We've **time to adjust**, so let's be sensible and not panic.
I'd say it to **anyone who asked**, farmer or not.
think: Five years is enough to **pay down the mortgage** with contracting money.
Robots come about when I'd be **stopping** anyway.
do: **Overpay the mortgage** with all hedge-cutting income every month.
Hire a **robot fencing** contractor once a neighbour proves it works.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to pay down the mortgage if I put every hedge-cutting penny into it.
fieldNote: Five years turns the threat into a **debt plan**.
Trades her **cushion** for faster repayment, a real gamble.
Would bring robots in where they **save her back**.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage with all hedge-cutting income
Hire a robot fencing contractor once a neighbour proves one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for robots. I'd be 71. That's well past my stopping time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everybody to plan, and farmers should use it. I'd say it calmly, because it is calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me time to sell Crag End on my own terms instead of the bank's. I'd stop farming around 66, before AGI even arrives. My only worry is the mortgage until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as I do until about 2034. Then I'd sell Crag End to a neighbour, clear the mortgage and buy a small house in the village with what's left. Ines has already said she'd help us look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Quite peaceful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still nagging you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether the land price holds. If it drops, there's less left after the bank. But that's normal farming worry, not robot worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I'd walk it on Sundays if the new owner lets me.

say: There's **time to plan**, and farmers should use it.
I'd say it **calmly**, because for me this picture really is calm.
think: I can sell **on my own terms**, not the bank's.
I'd stop around **66**, before AGI arrives.
My only worry until then is the **mortgage**.
do: **Sell** to a neighbour, clear the mortgage and buy a small village house.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to sell Crag End on my own terms instead of the bank's.
fieldNote: With a decade, her **exit plan** fits before AGI.
Lingering worry is **land price**, an ordinary farming concern.
Her calm is **real**, not just how she'd talk publicly.

steps.text: Keep farming Crag End until about 2034
Sell Crag End to a neighbour and clear the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be selling the family land in a hurry. What would help is a fair price for hill land and some government help for hill farms, because we look after the land as well as the sheep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how much farming depends on the weather. No AI changes the rain on Crag End. That's one thing I'm sure of.

headlineQuote: Hill farming is half weather and half stubbornness, and I've got plenty of both.
portrait: Freya, 58, owns a **hill farm** she inherited, with 400 ewes, 30 cows and a mortgage after a flood.
She earns extra from **hedge-cutting** and uses AI now and then for forms.
A steady adopter, she **waits for proof** from neighbours before buying anything.
Her main lever is the **land itself**: sell part fast, or all of it slowly.
Alarmed at **two years**, anxious at five, and at peace with a ten-year exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have to sell family land quickly to pay the bank.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair price** for hill land and government help for hill farms.
